study.title: 1 Corinthians 14 - Spiritual gifts, edification and order in worship
study.overview: Paul corrects the use of spiritual gifts in the Christian assembly, placing love as the main path and the building of the church as the decisive criterion for evaluating gifts. In this chapter, prophecy is preferred to languages because it communicates understanding, conviction, and comfort. Languages are not rejected, but must be used with interpretation and in a controlled manner, so that they do not produce confusion. The closure of the chapter insists that everything in worship must be done with decorum and order, reflecting the character of God, which is not of confusion, but of peace.

outline.title: Love, prophecy and the relative value of gifts
outline.explanation: Paul begins by linking this theme to the love of the previous chapter and guides the community to desire spiritual gifts, especially prophesy. Reason is practical: prophecy builds the church directly, while uninterpreted languages benefit the assembly.

outline.title: The problem of incomprehension and the need for understanding
outline.explanation: Paul uses simple comparisons - instruments without distinction of sound, speaks without clear meaning, foreigners without common language - to show that spiritual speech without understanding does not serve the collective. Therefore, he prefers few intelligible words to many incomprehensible words, even recognizing the personal value of strange language prayer when accompanied by understanding.

outline.title: Signs, discernment and order at church meeting
outline.explanation: Paul calls the church to maturity, applies the teaching of the Scriptures on tongues as a sign, and shows that the meeting should strengthen both believers and visitors. It regulates the use of tongues and prophecy: few speak, one interpret, others judge, and everything must contribute to building and peace.

outline.title: Silence, submission to apostolic authority and orderly worship
outline.explanation: Paul closes with difficult instructions about the silence of women in the church, asking for questions to be asked at home, and then corrects any attitude of spiritual superiority. No one should despise the apostolic order: the truly spiritual will recognize the word of the Lord; and the final summary is that everything be done decently and with order.

study.context: The notes indicate that, in the early Christian churches, the meeting was not conducted by professional clergy, but by shared participation, which explains why Paul regulates several simultaneous manifestations. The chapter responds to concrete disorder in the Corinthian assembly, where gifts were displayed in order to confuse the cult and weaken the collective building.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that spiritual gifts are not an end in themselves; their value is measured by the building up of the body of Christ. Prophecy is superior to languages in public worship because it communicates understandable truth, bringing instruction, convincing and comfort. Even when there is genuine spiritual manifestation, understanding remains important: the Christian faith does not celebrate meaningless ecstasy, but adoration with mind and spirit. Moreover, God desires peace and order in the church, so that spiritual freedom should never produce chaos. The excerpt about women should be read with caution and within the argument of the chapter, recognizing that there are different confessional interpretations about its scope and application; still, in the flow of the text, Paul seeks to preserve decorum, submission to authority and good testimony in the assembly.

scholarViews.insight: Prophecy is preferred because it brings more direct benefit to the church, while languages, without interpretation, are not immediately understandable or upbuilding to listeners.
Paul wants the worship to be intelligible so that the less educated can participate, say amen and be built up; therefore, he prefers few words with understanding to many without common benefit.
The closure of the chapter insists that every thing in worship must happen with reverence, in its proper place and time, because order is essential to religious life.

questions: In my participation in the church, do I seek to impress others or really build the brothers?
Are my words in public worship understandable and useful to the congregation, or just express something that only benefits me?
Have I treated order in worship as an expression of reverence to God, or as an obstacle to my personal preference?
study.practice: This week, evaluate your participation in the worship and church meetings by the criteria of building. If you have any gift of word, teaching, prayer or song, use it in a clear, humble and at the right time. Before you speak, ask: will this help the church to understand, believe, repent, be comforted or strengthened? Also practice listening carefully and valuing the order of worship as part of the peace that God wants to produce among his people.
study.uncertainty: There are important interpretative limitations in 1 Corinthians 14:34-35, especially on the scope of women's silence, for the text is debated between Christians and the given notes do not offer a detailed explanation beyond the affirmation of submission and decorum. There is also historical debate in the notes on the exact nature of languages; Adam Clarke mentions a specific hypothesis about Hebrew, but this appears as an interpretative proposal, not as a certainty of the biblical text. The rest of the application depends on the chapter flow and the notes provided.
